problemText: In his Fourteen Points address to Congress (January 1918), President Wilson's Point I opens: "Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view." This point is best understood as a direct response to which feature of the prewar European system that helped escalate a regional Balkan crisis into World War I?
choices: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo, the immediate trigger rather than an underlying cause
the German army's invasion of neutral Belgium in August 1914, which drew Britain into the war
the secret alliance treaties that helped escalate a regional Balkan crisis into a continental war
the mandate system that the Treaty of Versailles established over former German and Ottoman territories
hints: Point I targets 'private international understandings' — think about which prewar arrangement historians blame for turning a regional Balkan crisis into a continental war within about five weeks.
Rule out the assassination at Sarajevo (the immediate trigger, not what Point I targets) and the postwar mandate system (a later, separate issue covered by other items in this unit).

problemText: Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918), Point V, states that in adjusting colonial claims after the war, "the interests of the populations concerned must have equal weight with the equitable claims of the government whose title is to be determined." Which choice best states the principle this sentence commits Wilson to?
choices: that a colonized population's own interests should carry equal weight with the claims of its governing power
that every colonized territory would receive full political independence immediately once the war ended
that decisions about colonial claims would be made exclusively by a vote among the colonizing governments themselves
that Germany alone, as punishment for the war, would be required to surrender all of its colonial claims
hints: Look at exactly whose interests are said to carry 'equal weight' — the populations concerned, not just the claiming government.
This is a promise about HOW colonial claims would be adjusted (equal weighing), not a promise of immediate independence — don't overread the principle.

problemText: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles (1919) — commonly called the War Guilt Clause — states that "Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected" during the war. This clause served as the treaty's legal basis for which postwar demand on Germany?
choices: the permanent demilitarization of the Rhineland region along Germany's western border
the reparations payments the treaty subsequently required Germany to pay the victorious Allied powers
the mandate system that assigned former German colonies to Allied powers acting as trustees
the redrawing of Germany's eastern border to create the newly independent state of Poland
hints: 'Responsibility... for causing all the loss and damage' is the legal peg historians cite for a specific financial demand on Germany after the war.
Rule out Article 22's mandate system — that is a separate clause in a separate part of the same treaty (Part I, not Part VIII, where Article 231 sits).

problemText: Article 22 of the Covenant of the League of Nations, incorporated as Part I of the Treaty of Versailles (1919), describes former German and Ottoman territories as inhabited by "peoples not yet able to stand by themselves under the strenuous conditions of the modern world," and assigns their government to Allied powers so that, in the treaty's words, "this tutelage should be exercised by them as Mandatories on behalf of the League." Compared with Wilson's Fourteen Points promise that colonized populations' interests would carry equal weight with the claims of any governing power, Article 22's mandate language is best described as —
choices: a faithful implementation of Wilson's equal-weighing principle, applied and enforced through League of Nations diplomatic oversight
a punishment imposed only on Germany itself, with no application to any former Ottoman territory whatsoever
a temporary measure that ended all foreign administration of former German and Ottoman territories within five years
a guardianship arrangement that extended Allied imperial administration over the same territories under new legal terminology
hints: Compare 'equal weight with the equitable claims of the government' (Wilson's Point V) to 'tutelage... exercised... as Mandatories' (Article 22) — one treats local interests as a factor to weigh, the other assigns guardianship over supposedly incapable peoples.

Mandates went chiefly to Britain and France over former German colonies AND former Ottoman territories (e.g. Iraq, Palestine, Syria) — rule out any answer limiting this to Germany alone or claiming it matched Wilson's promise.

problemText: A described WWI-era Indian Army recruitment poster (Times Press, Bombay, catalogued by the Imperial War Museums) shows "a full-length Indian soldier in British Indian Army uniform, rifle held with bayonet fixed, standing in front of a large red-toned outline map of India" — and "A separate printed paper strip is pasted along the bottom edge of the sheet", letting the same base design be reissued with a locally translated caption across British India's many linguistic regions, part of a recruitment drive that "by the 1918 armistice had contributed more than 1.3 million men to Allied forces overseas, without the political self-determination promised elsewhere in wartime Allied propaganda". This poster and recruitment record are best used as evidence that —
choices: British India's colonial manpower was recruited on a mass scale without a matching grant of political self-rule
the Times Press produced a single, untranslated poster design identical across every linguistic region of British India
World War I was fought exclusively among European powers, entirely on European soil, with no other regions involved
the poster proves Indian nationalist leaders had already won a formal British promise of postwar independence by 1918
hints: The 1.3-million-man contribution and the phrase 'without the political self-determination promised' point to the colonial-manpower-without-political-return pattern covered earlier in this unit.
The poster's regional-language caption strips and India's massive troop contribution are direct evidence AGAINST treating World War I as a purely European conflict.

problemText: A described data table of Great Depression indicators reports that "the gold value of world trade fell by roughly 66 percent between 1929 and 1934, to about one-third of its 1929 level," a collapse the table attributes to falling commodity prices "on which many colonial and Latin American economies depended for export earnings, not merely a decline in industrial-country demand." This row of the table is best used as evidence against which claim?
choices: that world trade grew steadily during the early 1930s because of new international tariff-reduction agreements
that commodity prices for rubber, coffee, copper, and wheat rose sharply worldwide throughout the early 1930s
that the Great Depression's effects were confined mainly to industrialized economies such as the United States and Germany
that the Great Depression began with a banking crisis in Latin America before later spreading to the United States
hints: The row explicitly ties world trade's collapse to commodity-exporting 'colonial and Latin American economies' — not only to industrial powers like the US and Germany.
Rule out any answer describing rising trade or a Latin-American-origin crisis — the table describes a single US-centered contraction whose commodity-price effects then hit those economies hard.

problemText: The same data table reports that United States unemployment "rose from about 3 percent in 1929 to 24.9 percent in 1933," while German unemployment "rose to about 30 percent by 1932 (roughly 5.3 to 6 million workers), a rate that exceeded the American figure and reflected Germany's particular exposure to the withdrawal of short-term American loans after 1929." Read together, these two rows are best used as evidence that —
choices: German unemployment remained consistently below the American rate throughout the entire Great Depression period
a single US-centered credit contraction was transmitted through trade and finance into a second major industrial economy
the United States and Germany experienced entirely separate and unrelated economic crises during the early 1930s
German unemployment resulted mainly from the earlier, unrelated hyperinflation crisis of 1923, not from the American crash
hints: German unemployment (about 30%) actually EXCEEDED the US rate (24.9%) — rule out any answer claiming Germany's rate stayed lower throughout.
The passage explicitly links Germany's unemployment to 'the withdrawal of short-term American loans after 1929' — a direct transmission mechanism, not two unrelated national crises.

problemText: In his January 1941 address to Congress, President Roosevelt declares: "The first is freedom of speech and expression—everywhere in the world". Later in the same address, he defines freedom from fear as a reduction of armaments so thorough "that no nation will be in a position to commit an act of physical aggression against any neighbor—anywhere in the world". Delivered nearly a year before Pearl Harbor, FDR's freedom from fear is best read as a direct response to which development already covered in this unit?
choices: the formal United States declaration of war against Japan following the attack on Pearl Harbor
the New Deal's substantial expansion of the American federal government's role in managing the domestic economy
the mandate system that the Treaty of Versailles established over former German and Ottoman territories in 1919
the decade's earlier, unanswered aggressions in Manchuria, Ethiopia, and the Sudetenland that preceded the war
hints: The speech was delivered in January 1941 — nearly a year before Pearl Harbor and formal US entry into the war — so it cannot be responding to a declaration of war that hadn't happened yet.

'No nation... aggression against any neighbor' directly answers the decade's own unanswered aggressions (Manchuria, Ethiopia, the Sudetenland), not the earlier Versailles mandate issue from a previous topic in this unit.

problemText: Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, establishing the puppet state of Manchukuo, and began a full-scale war against China in 1937 following the Marco Polo Bridge Incident — both years before Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939, the conventional date historians use for World War II's start in Europe. This chronology is best used as evidence against which claim?
choices: that the League of Nations formally authorized and endorsed Japan's 1931 invasion of Manchuria
that Germany and Japan jointly planned a single, coordinated invasion timetable beginning as early as 1931
that World War II began in 1939 as a single, universal starting point for every region of the world
that Japan's war against China began only after the United States entered the war following Pearl Harbor in December 1941
hints: Manchuria (1931) and the full war with China (1937) both predate Pearl Harbor (December 1941) by years — the Asia-Pacific war did not begin with US entry into the war.
1939 marks the conventional start of the war in Europe specifically, not a universal global starting date — this chronology is the clearest counterexample.

problemText: Historians point to the Wannsee Conference (January 1942), where senior Nazi officials coordinated the bureaucratic machinery of the Holocaust; the Khmer Rouge regime's own documented administrative structure directing Cambodia's 1975-1979 killings; and years of documented extremist propaganda and organized militia training preceding Rwanda's 1994 genocide. Together, this evidence most directly refutes which claim about twentieth-century genocides?
choices: that these three genocides all occurred within the very same single decade of the twentieth century
that mass killings of this kind erupt spontaneously from pre-existing hatred rather than documented planning
that the Nuremberg Trials formally tried the organizers of all three genocides described in this passage
that international law took timely and effective action to prevent any of these three genocides before they began
hints: Each piece of evidence documents ADVANCE planning (a conference, an administrative structure, organized propaganda and training) — direct evidence against treating genocide as sudden, unplanned violence.
Rule out claims about international law's effectiveness or shared timing — the cited evidence specifically targets the 'spontaneous eruption' misconception, not those other claims.

problemText: The Nuremberg Trials (1945-1946) tried surviving senior Nazi officials before an international military tribunal. What key legal precedent did these trials establish?
choices: individuals, not just states, could be held criminally responsible for crimes against humanity, even when following orders
only entire nations, not individual military or political officials, could ever be held legally responsible for wartime atrocities
'following superior orders' was accepted at Nuremberg as a complete and sufficient legal defense against any war-crimes charge
the trials were conducted only by German judges appointed by the new postwar West German government itself
hints: Nuremberg's core precedent is individual criminal responsibility, even for officials acting under orders.

Rule out any answer denying individual responsibility, accepting 'following orders' as a full defense, or describing German-only judges — the tribunal included judges from the US, UK, USSR, and France.

problemText: The Nuremberg Trials were a judicial tribunal assigning individual criminal guilt for specific past acts, while the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) was a UN General Assembly declaration stating, in advance, a broad list of rights. Which statement best distinguishes these two institutions?
choices: both were binding international treaties enforced by the same international court
the UDHR only assigned specific criminal guilt to named Nazi officials, while Nuremberg articulated general aspirational rights
neither institution had any connection to the atrocities of World War II
Nuremberg was a retrospective judicial proceeding; the UDHR was a prospective, non-binding declaration of aspirational rights
hints: One institution judged specific past crimes; the other stated general principles for the future.
Rule out any answer treating both as binding treaties enforced by the same court, swapping their functions, or denying their WWII connection.

problemText: Colonial troops who fought for the Allied cause during the World Wars often invoked wartime rhetoric of freedom and self-determination on returning home. Which statement best explains how this experience contributed to postwar decolonization pressure?
choices: colonial veterans questioned why self-determination rhetoric justifying the war did not apply to their own countries
colonial troops who fought and returned home mostly voiced strong, continued support for European imperial rule
European governments granted full, immediate independence to every one of their colonies as a wartime service reward
colonial participation in the World Wars left no measurable trace on any postwar political movement in the colonies
hints: The gap between wartime rhetoric and colonized peoples' actual postwar treatment is the key mechanism here.
Rule out any answer claiming veterans supported continued imperial rule, that independence was immediately granted, or that there was no effect at all.

problemText: In response to the Great Depression, the United States expanded federal management of the economy through the New Deal, several Latin American states pursued import substitution industrialization, and Germany pursued autarky. Which statement best describes what these three responses had in common?
choices: each response sharply cut back international trade ties rather than pursuing closer global integration
each was a form of economic nationalism aimed at reducing dependence on a global trading system that had proven fragile
each was coordinated jointly among the United States, Latin American states, and Germany as a single international agreement
each response had no connection whatsoever to the Great Depression
hints: All three responses expanded state direction of the economy in reaction to a fragile, collapsed global trading system.
Rule out any answer describing a complete end to trade, a single joint international agreement, or no connection to the Depression.

problemText: Gandhi's 1930 Salt March, the 1919 May Fourth Movement, and Ho Chi Minh's 1919 petition to the Paris Peace Conference each responded to a similar gap between wartime promises and colonial reality, but through different methods and toward different immediate targets. Which statement best distinguishes Ho Chi Minh's 1919 petition from the Salt March?
choices: both actions were coordinated armed uprisings that directly attacked French colonial garrisons and British police outposts nationwide
Ho Chi Minh's 1919 petition secured France's immediate written agreement to grant full Vietnamese self-rule that year
Ho Chi Minh petitioned through diplomatic channels at an international conference, while the Salt March was mass civil disobedience against one policy
the Salt March was actually a formal diplomatic petition Gandhi submitted directly to the League of Nations in Geneva
hints: One action worked through formal diplomatic petition at an international conference; the other was direct, mass civil disobedience against a specific policy.
Rule out any answer describing armed uprisings, immediate Vietnamese independence, or swapping which leader used which method — neither matches the historical record.

problemText: Which event in the sequence of aggressions leading to World War II occurred earliest?
choices: Germany's invasion of Poland (1939)
the Munich Conference and annexation of the Sudetenland (1938)
Italy's invasion of Ethiopia (1935)
Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931)
hints: Japan's 1931 invasion of Manchuria predates each of the other three listed events by years.
Rule out Poland (1939), the Sudetenland (1938), and Ethiopia (1935) — all came later.

problemText: Historians continue to debate President Truman's decision to authorize the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Which statement best characterizes the nature of this ongoing historical debate?
choices: historians disagree over whether the bombings were necessary to avoid invasion, or whether Japan was near surrender
the debate was fully resolved decades ago by a unanimous historians' consensus that the bombings were unnecessary
historians broadly agree that the bombings were the only realistic way to end the Pacific War that year
the debate today concerns only the precise casualty count at Hiroshima, with no disagreement left about necessity
hints: The core disagreement is over necessity: avoiding a costly invasion versus a near-surrendering Japan and a signal to the USSR.
Rule out any answer claiming unanimous consensus in either direction, or narrowing the debate to casualty counts alone — the debate is fundamentally about necessity and motive.

problemText: Historians commonly summarize World War I's long-term structural causes using the acronym M.A.I.N. Which of the following correctly lists these four causes?
choices: Monarchy, Agriculture, Industry, Navigation
Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism
Migration, Autocracy, Isolationism, Neutrality
Mercantilism, Absolutism, Isolationism, and Nativism
hints: M.A.I.N. stands for four long-term structural causes historians cite for WWI's outbreak.
Rule out any answer using different words for the same letters — only one option matches the standard MAIN framework.

problemText: By 1914, Europe's major powers had divided into two competing alliance blocs: the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy). How did this alliance system contribute to turning the Austria-Serbia crisis into a continental war?
choices: the alliance system required all six powers to hold a unanimous vote before any member could declare war
the alliances had already fully dissolved by early 1914, leaving each great power to act on its own
mutual defense commitments meant one power's mobilization pulled its allies in too, turning a regional conflict continental
the alliance system bound its signatories only to economic cooperation and trade, with no shared military obligations
hints: Alliance commitments meant mobilization by one power triggered obligations for its partners, cascading outward.
Rule out any answer requiring a unanimous vote, claiming the alliances had dissolved, or limiting them to economic cooperation — none matches the actual system.

problemText: Gavrilo Princip's assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, is often cited as the event that started World War I. Which statement best describes the relationship between this assassination and the war's actual causes?
choices: the assassination was the sole cause of the war, with no meaningful role played by militarism, alliances, imperialism, or nationalism
the assassination is sometimes mistakenly dated to several months after the war had already fully begun
the assassination had no meaningful connection at all to the deeper causes of the war's outbreak
the assassination was the immediate trigger, while decades of militarism, alliances, rivalry, and nationalism were the deeper structural causes
hints: Distinguish a trigger (a single event) from underlying structural causes (decades-long trends).
Rule out any answer making the assassination the sole cause, misplacing its timing relative to the war, or denying any connection at all.

problemText: World War I produced casualties on a scale far beyond earlier European wars — the Battle of the Somme alone killed roughly a million soldiers. Which combination best explains this unprecedented death toll?
choices: industrial-era weapons such as machine guns, heavy artillery, and poison gas were used alongside tactics still based on nineteenth-century open-field infantry assaults
the war was fought mainly with pre-industrial weapons such as swords and cavalry lances, with few modern armaments involved
casualties were concentrated mainly among civilian populations, with only negligible military losses on any front
all major combatant nations had adopted trench-based defensive tactics specifically designed to minimize casualties
hints: The core mismatch was industrial-era firepower meeting outdated infantry tactics.

Rule out any answer describing pre-industrial weapons, casualties concentrated only among civilians, or tactics designed to minimize losses — trench warfare emerged in response to, not as a preventive measure against, this mismatch.
